newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Rodionov speaks soft, acts tough.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Rodionov speaks soft, acts tough.

text.p: General Igor Rodionov, who has quit the military to mark a new era of civilian control in Russia's defence ministry, is a soft-spoken but tough professional facing the daunting task of reforming the country's ailing armed forces.

His ultimate goal is to fulfil Yeltsin's decree of converting Russia's vast conscript army into a tighter professional force by the year 2000. More urgently, he has to secure his grip on the top brass and make sure servicemen are being paid and fed on time.
Yeltsin appointed Rodionov, then head of an elite military academy, in July after sacking the hawkish and unpopular Pavel Grachev.
His appointment, though advocated by the controversial Alexander Lebed -- then security chief -- was welcomed by all political forces, from communists to democrats.
The silver-haired general at first shunned media attention but a mountain of problems forced him to go public.
Trying to win more funds for the army, where servicemen had not been paid for months, Rodionov said in October:
"Russia's leadership and society should know that the chronic lack of funds is taking the armed forces to the brink of undesirable, and even uncontrollable, developments."
The warning struck home and he won a bigger share of funds in the 1997 budget, which is yet to be approved by parliament.
Rodionov has gradually replaced a considerable number of top brass, including the commander of paratroopers who opposed his reorganisation plans.

But he got himself into an awkward position with the Kremlin earlier this month when he apparently jumped the gun and said land forces commander General Vladimir Semyonov had been sacked for major violations.
The Kremlin has said Yeltsin had agreed to dismiss Semyonov but had not done so yet.
It was not the first time Rodionov found himself in an awkward spotlight.

Back in 1989, he earned the grim reputation of "Butcher of Tbilisi" in Georgia after Soviet troops under his command broke up a pro-independence rally in the Georgian capital with shovels, killing about 20 people.
Widely denounced, he kept silent over the incident and only much later officials exonerated him and said the true blame lay with the then-Soviet Georgian leaders.

Rodionov was quickly pulled out of Georgia after the Tbilisi scandal and transferred in 1990 to be head of the general staff's influential military academy -- a powerful post which means he knows the background of many of the rising stars in the Russian military.
The military widely respect Rodionov, a veteran of the Afghan war, as a professional, although he himself has previously said he should not be running the defence ministry.
In one interview Rodionov said he was in favour of Russia having a civilian defence minister, rather than a career military man such as himself.
Born on December 1, 1936, in the Penza region in central Russia, he graduated from the Orlov tank college, the Malinovsky armoured tank academy and the General Staff Military Academy.
He started out as a tank platoon commander and later saw active service in Afghanistan from 1985 to 1986 before becoming commander of Soviet forces in the Transcaucasus two years later.

In the final years of the Soviet Union, Rodionov was a member of the Soviet parliament, then called the Congress of People's Deputies, and was known as a vociferous critic of the foreign policy of reformist Communist leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
